missions.title: A damaged display item
paragraphs: A shop has only one desk lamp left. The display lamp has a visible scratch. The issue calls for a judgement about the relevant constraint and the effect of leaving it unresolved.

The recommendation is to ask about its condition and any available alternative. The expected benefit is that the customer can decide with complete information. The rationale should be explained to any stakeholder whose work or plans depend on the outcome.

The recommendation is stronger when its reasoning and its limits are both visible. The relevant stakeholder should be able to identify the immediate action, the assumption supporting it, and the condition that would justify reconsideration. Accountability includes checking whether the expected benefit actually materialises.

A purchase can appear attractive because one feature is easy to compare, such as the price or an advertised discount. Other features may be less visible: how well the item fits the intended use, what maintenance it requires, and what happens if it develops a fault. A good decision takes those less obvious costs into account without assuming that a higher price automatically means better quality.

Questions asked before payment also establish a clearer basis for any later conversation. The customer should distinguish a sales suggestion from a written guarantee, and a general return policy from an exception that applies to a particular product. If an item is damaged or incomplete, describing the issue accurately gives the seller a chance to offer a suitable solution. There is no need to turn every purchase into a long negotiation. The aim is simply to check the few details that matter most before making a commitment.
In a similar conversation, you could say: “Do you have this in a larger size?” “Thanks, I'm just looking at the moment.” “Can I try it on before I decide?”

missions.title: An apartment viewing time
paragraphs: A renter wants to see an apartment. The suggested viewing overlaps with work. The issue calls for a judgement about the relevant constraint and the effect of leaving it unresolved.

Within the agreed scope, the team can suggest two alternative viewing times. The expected benefit is that the agent can choose an available time. The rationale should be explained to any stakeholder whose work or plans depend on the outcome.

The action should be assessed against the purpose of the task and the needs of the people affected. A defensible decision remains open to revision when a material assumption changes. Documenting the reasoning creates a basis for learning and reduces the risk of repeating a process whose usefulness has not been established.

Choosing a place to live involves practical questions that may not be obvious during a short viewing. A room can look suitable while the surrounding arrangements create difficulties: unclear costs, limited access to shared facilities, or uncertainty about who handles repairs. Asking direct questions is not a sign of distrust. It gives everyone an opportunity to clarify expectations before those expectations become obligations.

Written information is particularly useful when more than one person manages the property. An assurance given during a viewing may otherwise be difficult to explain to someone who was not present. The same principle applies to an inventory: recording the condition of an item at the beginning protects both the resident and the owner from later confusion. A useful record should describe what is actually there, not what people assume ought to be there. Taking time to check details early can make later conversations shorter, calmer and easier to resolve.

In a similar conversation, you could say: “What's included in the rent, and what do I pay separately?” “Could we arrange a viewing for Saturday morning?” “When would it be available for someone to move in?”

missions.title: A clearer repair request
paragraphs: A customer reports a problem with a washing machine. The first message only says that it does not work. The issue calls for a judgement about the relevant constraint and the effect of leaving it unresolved.

A proportionate response would be to describe what happens when the machine is switched on. The expected benefit is that the repair service can understand the reported problem. The rationale should be explained to any stakeholder whose work or plans depend on the outcome.

The expected benefit should be treated as a proposition to evaluate, rather than as an automatic consequence of agreement. Any material assumption needs to be explicit, and the people affected should know how an unresolved dependency will be handled. If the response falls short, the team should review the evidence and revise the approach.

A service visit usually involves more than the visible repair. Someone has to identify the problem, arrange access, decide what work is authorised and confirm whether additional parts are needed. If these responsibilities remain unclear, a visit can end without a useful result even when the person doing the work is capable and well prepared.

A quotation should therefore be understood as an explanation of proposed work, not merely a number to accept or reject. It helps to ask what the price includes and which circumstances could change it. If a further problem is discovered, the customer should know whether work will pause until approval is given. Completion also deserves a clear check. The relevant question is not only whether the visitor has finished, but whether the original problem has been resolved and the customer understands what to do next. That final conversation can prevent an unnecessary second visit.
In a similar conversation, you could say: “What time should I expect you tomorrow morning?” “How much will it cost, including the new part?” “Is there anything I need to do before you arrive?”

missions.title: A clearer job application
paragraphs: An applicant prepares a short introduction. The first draft does not mention the skills requested in the advertisement. The issue calls for a judgement about the relevant constraint and the effect of leaving it unresolved.

A proportionate response would be to connect the introduction to the role requirements. The expected benefit is that the employer can see why the application is relevant. The rationale should be explained to any stakeholder whose work or plans depend on the outcome.

The expected benefit should be treated as a proposition to evaluate, rather than as an automatic consequence of agreement. Any material assumption needs to be explicit, and the people affected should know how an unresolved dependency will be handled. If the response falls short, the team should review the evidence and revise the approach.

Applying for work requires a balance between presenting experience confidently and making claims that can be supported. Broad descriptions such as hardworking or a good communicator are easy to write but difficult for an employer to evaluate. A specific example gives the reader something more useful: a situation, an action and an outcome that can be discussed further.

The same care should apply to practical arrangements. An invitation to interview may include unfamiliar instructions, a different time zone or a request for additional documents. Checking those details does not weaken the application; it shows that the candidate is taking the process seriously. Questions about working hours or responsibilities can also help both sides assess whether the position is a realistic fit. A successful application is not simply one that creates a favourable impression. It should also allow the applicant and the employer to make a better-informed decision about working together.

In a similar conversation, you could say: “I'm interested in the role and would like to learn more.” “Could you tell me a little more about the working hours?” “Thank you for getting back to me about the interview.”

missions.title: A missing handover owner
paragraphs: A colleague starts a new task during a handover. Nobody has agreed who will answer later questions. The issue calls for a judgement about the relevant constraint and the effect of leaving it unresolved.

Within the agreed scope, the team can name a contact for follow-up questions. The expected benefit is that the colleague can get clarification when needed. The rationale should be explained to any stakeholder whose work or plans depend on the outcome.

The action should be assessed against the purpose of the task and the needs of the people affected. A defensible decision remains open to revision when a material assumption changes. Documenting the reasoning creates a basis for learning and reduces the risk of repeating a process whose usefulness has not been established.

A handover is a transfer of understanding as well as responsibility. Passing on a folder or forwarding an email does not guarantee that another person can recognise what is urgent, what has already been decided, or which apparent fact is still an assumption. A useful handover makes those distinctions visible.

The information should be organised around the next person's decisions, not merely around the order in which events happened. For each unfinished item, it helps to identify the current position, the next action and the person responsible. Old information should be clearly marked so that it does not compete with an updated instruction. There should also be a chance to ask questions before the original owner becomes unavailable. This may feel slower than sending a quick message, but it reduces the time someone else would otherwise spend reconstructing the situation. The final test is whether the recipient can explain what they will do next and why.
In a similar conversation, you could say: “Where did we leave off before the shift changed?” “Thanks for the update. I'll take it from here.” “Is there anything else I should know before you leave?”
